verdict: Caution: lend selectively to organised modular/interior-fitout units with verifiable order books and tight monthly monitoring; avoid pure commodity solid-wood job-work units exposed to Rajasthan's demand slowdown.
title: Jodhpur Wooden & Modular Furniture: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Jodhpur's furniture cluster runs on solid-wood and handicraft job-work plus a growing modular/interior-fitout layer, converting timber and boards into made-to-order pieces.** Cash comes in on order confirmation and dispatch, not on production; value sits in design, finishing and installation rather than in the raw plank. The cluster is fragmented and unorganised-dominated, so individual units are price-takers on commodity lines [9]. Peer Dhabriya confirms the same split nationally: many unorganised and even big organised players in modular furniture, with differentiation only through design and execution [6].

## Where cash and value sit
**Working capital is the whole game: timber/board inventory plus a receivable tail from builders and institutional buyers.** Capex is modest for job-work shops but jumps for anyone doing panel processing or modular fitout. Pricing power exists only where the unit owns design and installation; commodity solid-wood work is bid down. So when a proposal lands, check the receivable ageing by buyer type and the inventory days on timber; if receivables are concentrated in one builder, ask for the buyer's payment track record and stage-wise billing.

## What has changed now
**Rajasthan itself is the weak spot: state GST collections are -4.7% Apr-to-date against India +6.1%, and electricity demand +4.0% versus India +9.5% [D].** That is a local demand signal, not a national one — India-wide IIP for furniture (NIC 31) is +9.4% YoY and +7.4% Apr-to-date [D]. Local news on the Jodhpur cluster is thin; the sources are directory and blog pages, not transaction data [1][2][3], so lean on first principles and peers here. Peer results are healthy — Greenply Q2FY27 topline +16.1% YoY, EBITDA margin 11.2% [7]; Dhabriya net profit +100.52% in the December 2025 quarter and a Rs 25.30 crore Godrej order [4]. Note the Dhabriya figures are undated in the source and the Greenply call is Q3-2026, so treat both as directional.

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
**Pursue organised modular/interior-fitout units with design capability and multi-city or institutional order books; avoid pure commodity solid-wood job-work with single-buyer dependence.** Structure as cash-flow lending against verified orders, with a charge on receivables and stock. Take monthly: GST returns, receivable ageing by buyer, order-book position, and stock statements. Covenant a debt/equity ceiling — peers run conservative, Greenply targets below 0.6x [5], Omfurn at 0.29x with 3.39x interest cover [11]. If a unit cannot show buyer-wise ageing, ask for bank statements and GST 2A/2B reconciliation before sanction.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for GST turnover falling below bank credits, receivable days stretching past the buyer's stated terms, and inventory build in slow-moving designs.** If monthly GST falls two months running, cut limits and ask for the order book. If a single buyer crosses a third of receivables, seek diversification or buyer confirmation. If interest cover drops toward peer floor levels, reprice or exit.
